Janet: Ferdinand?
Ferdinand: Janet! We're finally connected. Thanks for calling back.
Janet: I've been worried. Are you alright?
Ferdinand: Calm down, Janet. I'm fine. I only have a minute's privacy on this phone. I was reviewing public response to the fashion show ... and by complete coincidence, I came across a terrible, disturbing rumor. Just like that - and out of the blue. I hope it won't lead to a real scandal. I'll admit it needs to be checked out.

Janet: Go on.
Ferdinand: The writer claims that Holly's clothing is outsourced to South East Asia and child labor is used in their factories.
Janet: What? Ferdinand, how credible did this source seem?
Ferdinand: I have no idea. It seems to have come out of nowhere. There isn't a lot of information to back it up. The claim is based on hearsay. But Holly's is the only company that is mentioned by the writer.
Janet: Who is the writer? We need to figure out who she is and …
Ferdinand: Janet ... I'll ask around. The writer's whole purpose was to call people to action, starting with petitions and boycotts.

Janet: This is too weird. Ferdinand, the truth on this matter needs to be investigated. Facts and evidence are needed above all.
Ferdinand: I agree. By good chance I know a reporter in Rio with great connections.
Janet: Good. Finances are not be considered when dealing with this matter. Can I count on you, Ferdinand?
Ferdinand: Absolutely. Thanks Janet. I'm on to it. I won't let you down.

Phrasal verbs consist of a verb and one or more prepositions. They are common, especially in spoken English. The meaning of phrasal verbs is often completely different from the meaning of the verb alone. Phrasal verbs can either be separable or inseparable.
Separable phrasal verbs consist of two parts. They always require an object.
The object of a phrasal verb can go either between the verb and the preposition or after the preposition.

Examples:
I figured out what happened.
I figured it out.
If the object of the sentence is a pronoun, it must go between the two parts of the phrasal verb.

Example:
I figured it out. > NOT > I figured out it.
Some phrasal verbs are inseparable, so the verb must be directly followed by its preposition. Otherwise, the meaning of the phrasal verb will be incorrect.
Some inseparable phrasal verbs never use an object.

Examples:
Can I count on you?
I checked out the matter.
I came across a terribly disturbing rumor.
I'll admit it needs to be checked out.
It seems to have come out of nowhere.
We need to figure out who she is.
There's isn't a lot of information to back it up.

Sentence stress gives English its rhythm or "beat".
Word stress is emphasis on one syllable within a word.
Sentence stress is emphasis on certain words within a sentence.
Most sentences have two basic types of words:

Content Words
  • Content words are the important or key words in a sentence. They provide the meaning of the sentence.

Structure Words
  • Structure words are not important words. They are small words that you use to make the sentence correct.
When you want to stress new information, you use different intonation and stress on the “new” word or idea. Usually, the stressed words in a sentence are the nouns, verbs, adjectives and adverbs.
Sometimes, you can choose to stress other types of words to show that you are adding new information or when talking about a strange event.
Child labor is used in their factories!
